todays_goal: After Math, use clear age-appropriate questions while keeping real academic vocabulary. French fixes one grammar pattern; Science strengthens the lens model; History advances the war; Literature and Writing focus on perspective and evidence; Builder Lab stays laptop-only with whiteboard coaching.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Atticus already chooses être and avoir well. The remaining gap is using de/d' after pas.
lessons.course_context: Fix one small grammar pattern before adding new grammar.
lessons.why_it_matters: When this pattern becomes automatic, speaking and writing French becomes easier.

vocabulary.definition: saying that someone does not have something

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: today you are fixing one small pattern. After pas, use de, or d' before a vowel sound. Say each sentence out loud before you write it. Example: J'ai un livre -> Je n'ai pas de livre.

worked_examples.title: Example 1
worked_examples.explanation: Un changes to de after pas.

worked_examples.title: Example 2
worked_examples.explanation: Use d' before a vowel sound.

independent_practice.prompt: Make this negative: J'ai un stylo.
Make this negative: Elle a des devoirs.
Make this negative: Nous avons une voiture.
Make this negative: Ils ont des livres.
Make this negative: Tu as un chien.
Make this negative: Il a un ordinateur.
Make this negative: Vous avez une question.
Make this negative: Elles ont des calculatrices.
Make this negative: J'ai une sœur.
Make this negative: Nous avons des devoirs.

exit_ticket.prompt: Get at least 9 out of 10 correct. Fix any mistake and say the corrected sentence aloud.
exit_ticket.answer: At least nine correct de/d' transformations.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. Keep wording short and clear. Teach the one pattern first: ne/n' + avoir + pas + de/d' + noun. Use the whiteboard for the pattern and one different example. If Atticus asks what a word means, explain it in plain language in one sentence and return to the task. Do not add extra grammar. If he uses un/une/des after pas, say: Check the noun after pas. Then require the full corrected sentence.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: Atticus understands that lenses redirect light but still needs a secure curved-lens and focal-point model.
lessons.course_context: Repair the lens model, then apply it to cameras and the eye.
learning_objectives: Explain why a curved lens changes light paths.
Draw parallel rays bending toward a focal point.
Explain what a camera lens and eye lens do.
lessons.why_it_matters: The same idea explains cameras, eyes, microscopes, and telescopes.

vocabulary.definition: a lens thicker in the middle
light changing direction when it moves between materials
where parallel rays meet in a simple lens model
the light-sensitive back part of the eye
the light-detecting part of a digital camera

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: a convex lens is curved, not flat. Light hits different parts of the curved lens at different angles. The rays change direction as they enter and leave the lens. This can make the rays meet near a focal point. A camera sends light toward a sensor. Your eye sends light toward the retina.

worked_examples.title: Camera
worked_examples.problem: How does a camera lens help make an image?
worked_examples.solution: It bends incoming rays toward the sensor.
worked_examples.explanation: The curved lens redirects the light into an organized image pattern.

worked_examples.title: Eye
worked_examples.problem: Where does the eye lens send light?
worked_examples.explanation: The retina detects the light pattern.

guided_practice.prompt: Draw a convex lens. Add three parallel rays. Show them bending toward the same area. Label the focal point.

independent_practice.prompt: Why does the lens being curved change the way the light moves?
How does a camera lens help make an image?
Where does the eye lens send light?
A student says, The eye lens makes the object bigger. What does the lens really do?

exit_ticket.prompt: Why does the curved shape of a convex lens matter?
exit_ticket.answer: The curved shape makes rays hit the boundary at different angles, so they bend by different amounts.

exit_ticket.prompt: In 2 sentences, explain how either a camera OR your eye uses a lens.
exit_ticket.answer: The lens bends incoming light. It directs the rays toward a sensor or retina so an image can be detected.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach first. Speak directly to Atticus and keep questions short. Use whiteboard_draw to build the lens diagram one step at a time: principal axis, convex lens, three incoming rays, bent rays, focal point. Ask one short check after each step. If Atticus asks what a word means, define it simply and continue. For assigned questions, do not draw the completed answer; use a different example or blank scaffold.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.lesson_title: The War Begins: Athens, Sparta, Strategy, and Plague
lessons.previous_learning: Atticus did strong work on the causes of the Peloponnesian War.
lessons.course_context: Move from why the war began to how the two sides fought and what the plague changed.
learning_objectives: Compare Spartan land strength with Athenian naval strength.
Explain why Athens used the Long Walls and port.
Explain one benefit and one cost of Pericles's plan.
lessons.why_it_matters: History is about how strengths, choices, geography, and surprises affect what happens next.

vocabulary.definition: a plan for how to reach a goal
walls that linked Athens to its port
when a plan helps in one way but causes a cost or risk
a deadly disease spreading through many people

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: Sparta had the stronger land army. Athens had the stronger navy. Athens avoided a big land battle, stayed behind the walls, and used the port for supplies. That helped against Sparta, but it also crowded many people together. Then a plague hit Athens and caused serious losses.

worked_examples.title: One plan, two effects
worked_examples.problem: What did the Long Walls help and hurt?
worked_examples.solution: They helped protect Athens from a land attack but increased crowding.
worked_examples.explanation: A plan can solve one problem and create another.

independent_practice.prompt: Why did Athens try to avoid a big land battle with Sparta?
How did the Long Walls and the port help Athens?
What did Pericles's plan HELP with?
What new problem did the plan create?
Why was the plague bad for Athens besides killing many people?
Was Pericles's plan a bad plan just because the plague happened? Explain your answer.

exit_ticket.prompt: In 4-5 sentences, explain how Sparta's strength, Athens's strength, and the plague affected the early war.
exit_ticket.answer: A strong answer explains Sparta land strength, Athens naval/Long Wall strategy, and how plague hurt Athens.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach before questioning. Speak directly to Atticus. Keep question wording simple. Use whiteboard_draw for a simple map: Athens, Piraeus, Long Walls, sea, Sparta outside. Add arrows for land pressure and sea supply. Then make a two-column chart: HELPED / CAUSED A NEW PROBLEM. If Atticus asks what a word means, answer in plain language and continue. Do not draw assigned answers.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.previous_learning: Atticus is strong at inference and theme but questions should not be harder to read than the idea being tested.
lessons.course_context: Use clear questions to teach fact, perspective, tone, and a more nuanced explanation.
learning_objectives: Tell the difference between a fact and a perspective.
Explain what a character thinks and why.
lessons.why_it_matters: Strong readers notice that two people can see the same facts and explain them differently.

vocabulary.definition: how a person sees or understands something
the attitude you hear in someone's words
something that happened in the story

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: a fact is what happened. A perspective is what a person thinks the fact means. Two people can see the same fact and explain it differently.

worked_examples.title: Fact vs perspective
worked_examples.problem: The power fails after the balcony lights turn on.
worked_examples.solution: The timing is a fact. What caused it is the characters' interpretation.
worked_examples.explanation: Evidence and interpretation are not the same.

independent_practice.prompt: What problem are Nadia and Marcus trying to solve?
What does Nadia think is causing the problem at first?
What makes Marcus think the balcony lights matter?
What does “That proves nothing” tell you about Nadia's attitude?
How does Nadia sound different at the end?
Why is Nadia's final idea better than her first idea?
Write one lesson or theme from the story.
Give TWO story details that support your theme. Tell why each detail matters.
Write a 3-sentence summary of what happened.

exit_ticket.prompt: In one sentence, explain the difference between a fact and a character's perspective.
exit_ticket.answer: A fact is what happened; a perspective is what a character thinks the fact means.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. Keep question wording simple and short. If useful, draw a three-column whiteboard table: FACT / NADIA THINKS / MARCUS THINKS. If he asks what a word means, define it simply and return to the story. If he tells what happened when the question asks why it matters, ask: Why is that important? Do not answer assigned questions.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: Atticus has strong ideas but sometimes stops before fully explaining why evidence matters.
lessons.course_context: Use simple prompts but keep high standards for evidence, reasoning, and revision.
lessons.why_it_matters: Clear writing makes your thinking easy for another person to follow.

vocabulary.definition: the exact thing that happened or was said
why the evidence helps prove your answer

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: use a simple pattern. CLAIM = your answer. EVIDENCE = the exact detail. REASONING = why the detail matters. A good paragraph uses this pattern more than once and ends with a conclusion.

worked_examples.title: Evidence + reasoning
worked_examples.problem: Nadia changes her mind after the lights fail again.
worked_examples.solution: The lights fail seven seconds after Marcus turns the balcony spots back on. That timing supports his idea that the electrical load matters.
worked_examples.explanation: The reasoning tells what the evidence proves.

independent_practice.prompt: Make this more exact: Nadia was stubborn. Use one line or action from the story.
Why does your detail matter?
Make this sentence clearer: Both of them were right because there were two causes.
Write 7-9 sentences: Why is Nadia's final explanation better than her first one? Use TWO exact details. After each detail, explain why it matters. End with a conclusion.

exit_ticket.prompt: Before you finish: Did you answer the question, use two exact details, explain both, and end with a conclusion?
exit_ticket.answer: A complete revised paragraph satisfying all four checks.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. Keep wording short. Do not dictate sentences. If he asks what a word means, define it simply and continue. If evidence is vague, ask: What exact thing happened or was said? If reasoning is missing, ask: Why does that detail matter? Use the whiteboard for a different CLAIM -> EVIDENCE -> WHY IT MATTERS example.
